import os

DATABASE_HOST = os.environ.get(
"DATABASE_HOST",
"localhost"
)

DATABASE_USER = os.environ["DATABASE_USER"]

DATABASE_PASSWORD = os.environ[
"DATABASE_PASSWORD"
]

Now the application can use different settings in development, testing, and production without modifying its source code.

For example:

export DATABASE_HOST="db.internal"
export DATABASE_USER="app_user"
export DATABASE_PASSWORD="your-secret"

Environment variables are useful, but they aren't automatically a complete secrets-management solution.

For sensitive production credentials, consider using a dedicated secrets manager, restricting access, and rotating credentials regularly.

Lesson: Configuration should change between environments without requiring code changes.

  1. Successful Execution Doesn't Mean Correct Results

This is one of the most dangerous problems in data-processing applications.

Imagine a web scraper that collects product information.

The script runs successfully.

No exceptions occur.

The output file is created.

Everything looks fine.

Except the file contains only 8 products instead of the expected 200.

Technically, the program completed.

But from a business perspective, it failed.

This is especially common in web scraping, ETL pipelines, API integrations, and scheduled data-processing jobs.

Validate the output

def validate_products(products):
if not isinstance(products, list):
raise TypeError(
"Expected a list of products"
)

if not products:
    raise ValueError(
        "No products were collected"
    )

for index, product in enumerate(products):
    if not isinstance(product, dict):
        raise TypeError(
            f"Invalid product at index {index}"
        )

    required_fields = {
        "id",
        "name",
        "price"
    }

    missing = required_fields - product.keys()

    if missing:
        raise ValueError(
            f"Product {index} is missing: {missing}"

Duplicate records.

Unexpectedly low record counts.

Missing identifiers.

Data freshness.

Sudden changes in price distributions.

A nonempty list is not proof that a scraping job succeeded.

And a zero exit code is not proof that the business requirements were satisfied.

Lesson: Validate outcomes, not just execution.

Let's imagine a Python application processing 10,000 products.

After processing 8,500 products, the server restarts.

What happens next?

If the application starts from the beginning, it might repeat thousands of operations.

If it doesn't save progress, some data could be lost.

This is where a simple script starts becoming a reliable system.

A basic approach is to track completed product identifiers.

import json

"completed_products.json"
)

if not CHECKPOINT_FILE.exists():
return set()

    "r",
    encoding="utf-8"

    return set(json.load(file))

temporary = CHECKPOINT_FILE.with_suffix(

    "w",
    encoding="utf-8"

Does the application validate its output?

title: How to Bulk Download YouTube Transcripts for RAG and AI Summaries (Python)
summary:
Getting one YouTube transcript is easy. Getting 500 of them for a RAG pipeline, a research project or a weekly channel digest is where things get annoying.

In this post we show a simple way to pull transcripts in bulk with Python, get clean JSON back, and split the text into chunks ready for embeddings.

The usual options

Copy from the YouTube UI. Fine for one video. Not an option for a channel.

The official YouTube Data API. It can list captions, but downloading caption tracks only works for videos you own. For public videos from other channels it does not help.

Open source libraries like youtube-transcript-api. Great for local scripts. The catch: YouTube often blocks requests from cloud and datacenter IPs, so the same code that works on your laptop starts failing on a server or in a scheduled job. The library docs themselves describe this and suggest using proxies.

A hosted scraper. You send a list of videos or a channel URL and get structured data back. Someone else deals with blocks, retries and format changes. This is what we use below.

Bulk download with Python

We will use our YouTube Transcript Scraper on Apify. You need a free Apify account and an API token (Console > Settings > API & Integrations).

pip install apify-client

from apify_client import ApifyClient

client = ApifyClient("YOUR_APIFY_TOKEN")

run_input = {
    "videos": [
        "https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Pba4OZjn3cY",
        "https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=46v8M4RsCzg",
        "https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tu6tF-lVDJI",
    ],
    "language": "en",
}

run = client.actor("wiseus-labs/youtube-transcript-scraper").call(run_input=run_input)

items = client.dataset(run["defaultDatasetId"]).list_items().items
for item in items:
    print(item["status"], item["title"], len(item.get("text") or ""))

Want a whole channel instead of a list? Swap the input:

run_input = {
    "channelOrPlaylistUrls": ["https://www.youtube.com/@TED"],
    "maxVideosPerSource": 50,
    "language": "en",
}

Playlists work the same way.

What you get back

One row per video:

{
  "videoId": "Pba4OZjn3cY",
  "title": "Why It's So Hard to Listen When You Disagree | Emily Kasriel | TED",
  "language": "en",
  "captionType": "manual",
  "status": "ok",
  "segmentCount": 194,
  "text": "You know, there's something quite strange going on...",
  "url": "https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Pba4OZjn3cY"
}

captionType tells you whether the track was written by a human (manual) or generated by YouTube (auto). Timestamped segments come in the segments field if you need to link answers back to a moment in the video.

Videos without subtitles do not crash the run. They come back with status: "no_captions", so you can filter them out.

Chunk it for RAG

Most embedding models work better with chunks of a few hundred words than with a 10,000 word transcript. A minimal splitter:

def chunk_text(text, size=300, overlap=50):
    words = text.split()
    step = size - overlap
    return [" ".join(words[i:i + size]) for i in range(0, len(words), step)]

docs = []
for item in items:
    if item["status"] != "ok":
        continue
    for n, chunk in enumerate(chunk_text(item["text"])):
        docs.append({
            "id": f'{item["videoId"]}-{n}',
            "text": chunk,
            "source": item["url"],
            "title": item["title"],
        })

print(len(docs), "chunks ready for embeddings")

From here, send docs to your vector store of choice. Keeping source and title on every chunk means your chatbot can cite the exact video it answered from.

What it costs

$1.50 per 1,000 transcripts on the Apify Free plan, less on paid plans. Videos without subtitles and failed videos are not charged. The free plan includes $5 of monthly credit, which covers a few thousand transcripts.

No code option

If you do not want to write any code, open the ready-made task, paste your video links and press Start. Results export to CSV, JSON or Excel:

  • Download YouTube transcripts in bulk from a list of videos
  • Download all transcripts from a YouTube channel

The Actor page with all options: YouTube Transcript Scraper.

If something breaks or you need a field we do not return yet, open an issue on the Actor page. We read all of them.

title: I built a terminal multiplexer for coding agents that works on my phone
summary:
Disclosure: drafted with AI help from my own notes and posts, and checked against the repo.

I run a lot of coding agents at once, mostly Claude Code and Codex, across several projects. Running them was never the problem. The problems were everything around them: too many windows, agents leaving hung processes behind, no way to tell which one was waiting on me, and having to remote into my desktop or SSH into a single shell to deal with any of it from my phone. Even then, a terminal on a phone couldn't show me the frontend I needed to check.

I tried Orca and herdr. Both were better than what I had. Neither had a real markdown notes editor, and neither had a phone interface I could actually work in. So I built swe-mux.

What it is

A terminal multiplexer. It runs any shell or CLI in real terminals on your own machine and serves the same live sessions to your desktop and your phone. Claude Code, Codex, opencode, pi and oh-my-pi get a live status (working, done, or waiting on you), searchable history and resume. Anything else runs as an ordinary terminal with everything except the status.

It's the actual terminal, not a UI wrapped around the agent. You can use it as a plain terminal, or start claude in a shell and that pane becomes an agent session.

On the desktop it's tabs and panes of sessions, notes, files and dev-server previews. Shift+Enter, Ctrl+Backspace, paste and click-to-position behave the same in every agent, shortcuts come from tmux, VS Code, Vim or Emacs presets, and images paste straight from the clipboard.

Status

Status comes from three places: the CLI's hooks, its transcript, and the terminal itself. No single one of them reliably tells "waiting on you" apart from "busy in the background", so it uses all three. You pick which events alert you and how, a sound on the desktop and a push notification on the phone, with quiet hours and separate desktop and mobile settings.

The phone

The same sessions, over your own Tailscale network, installed as a PWA. The terminal with a usable keyboard and a key rail for the keys a phone keyboard doesn't have, git diff review, files, notes, and a push notification when an agent needs a decision.

A dev server bound to 127.0.0.1 on the host is proxied through swe-mux, so the phone opens it without another port being exposed. Being able to play-test and check a frontend on the phone is what closed the development loop there for a lot of my projects. I can work from anywhere now, and I do.

Your tailnet policy is the access control. There's no separate swe-mux login, so any device your tailnet admits gets a terminal on your machine. Treat it like SSH.

Two things I use constantly

A prompt queue, so the thing I think of mid-turn waits until the agent is actually done instead of interrupting it.

Messages between sessions, so a Codex session can ask a Claude session something. I don't want my workflow tied to one provider.

Notes

Notes, and any markdown file in a project, open in the same WYSIWYG editor on desktop and phone, and they autosave. No more notes scattered across different places.

Sessions survive updates

A separate supervisor process owns the terminals, so the daemon can restart and the app can update underneath them without killing anything. I update it several times a day. My own daemon started 615 times across the 98 days its log covers, so this was never optional.

It has limits. A reboot, a power loss or the supervisor itself crashing still ends the live processes. What survives those is the transcript and enough state to resume each agent.

Limits

It was built on Windows, which is where I use it every day and the only platform with a packaged desktop app. The installer is unsigned, so SmartScreen warns on first run; the PyPI install avoids that. macOS and Linux run the daemon and use a browser. CI runs all three, and I've tested Linux myself, but I haven't lived on macOS.

There's no swe-mux account, no server of mine in the path, and no telemetry. The agents still talk to their own providers, and there's a once-a-day update check you can turn off in Settings.

Try it

The demo is the real interface with simulated agents, nothing to install.

Install with uv tool install swe-mux (or pipx install swe-mux), then run swe-mux on Windows or swemux start elsewhere. It's Apache-2.0: github.com/jatoran/swe-mux.

I've put a lot of work into the first run. Where the install or the first hour goes wrong is the feedback I want most.

The same sessions, over your own Tailscale network, installed as a PWA. The terminal with a usable keyboard and a key rail for the keys a phone keyboard doesn't have, git diff review, files, notes, and a push notification when an agent needs a decision.

A dev server bound to 127.0.0.1 on the host is proxied through swe-mux, so the phone opens it without another port being exposed. Being able to play-test and check a frontend on the phone is what closed the development loop there for a lot of my projects. I can work from anywhere now, and I do.

Your tailnet policy is the access control. There's no separate swe-mux login, so any device your tailnet admits gets a terminal on your machine. Treat it like SSH.

Two things I use constantly

A prompt queue, so the thing I think of mid-turn waits until the agent is actually done instead of interrupting it.

Messages between sessions, so a Codex session can ask a Claude session something. I don't want my workflow tied to one provider.

Notes

Notes, and any markdown file in a project, open in the same WYSIWYG editor on desktop and phone, and they autosave. No more notes scattered across different places.

Sessions survive updates

A separate supervisor process owns the terminals, so the daemon can restart and the app can update underneath them without killing anything. I update it several times a day. My own daemon started 615 times across the 98 days its log covers, so this was never optional.

It has limits. A reboot, a power loss or the supervisor itself crashing still ends the live processes. What survives those is the transcript and enough state to resume each agent.

Limits

It was built on Windows, which is where I use it every day and the only platform with a packaged desktop app. The installer is unsigned, so SmartScreen warns on first run; the PyPI install avoids that. macOS and Linux run the daemon and use a browser. CI runs all three, and I've tested Linux myself, but I haven't lived on macOS.

There's no swe-mux account, no server of mine in the path, and no telemetry. The agents still talk to their own providers, and there's a once-a-day update check you can turn off in Settings.

The demo is the real interface with simulated agents, nothing to install.

Install with uv tool install swe-mux (or pipx install swe-mux), then run swe-mux on Windows or swemux start elsewhere. It's Apache-2.0: github.com/jatoran/swe-mux.

title: We Open-Sourced Our AI Subtitle Translation Engine: Every SRT Cue In, Every Cue Out
summary:
If you've ever pasted an SRT file into an LLM and asked for a translation, you've probably seen this: you send 400 subtitle cues and get back 397. Two short lines got merged into one sentence, one line disappeared, and from that point on every translation sits on the wrong timestamp. The output looks fine at a glance, and you only notice when the dialogue on screen no longer matches what people are saying.

We hit this problem constantly while building GeekLink's subtitle translator, so we pulled the core engine out and open-sourced it under GPL-3.0: jev-subtitle-translator.

Why LLMs mangle subtitles

LLMs are trained to write fluent text, and subtitles aren't fluent text. A single sentence often spans three cues, a cue can be just "Yeah." or "—no!", and a model that's trying to be helpful will happily join fragments into natural sentences. Ask it to "keep the format" and it mostly will, until a batch of 40 cues comes back with 38 items and nothing tells you which two are gone.

Prompt engineering alone doesn't fix this. You need structure the model can't drift away from, plus validation that doesn't trust the model's output.

How the engine handles it

The pipeline looks like this:

Parse SRT and preserve every cue
        ↓
Translate ID-tagged batches
        ↓
Validate returned IDs and non-empty translations
        ↓
Retry only missing or empty IDs
        ↓
Run deterministic checks and Jev review
        ↓
Rebuild the SRT from the original cue list

A few design decisions do most of the work:

Timestamps never reach the model. The SRT is parsed locally. Subtitle numbers, order, and timestamps stay on your machine. Only the dialogue text and a stable ID per cue are sent to the model.

Structured output, not prose. Each batch is translated with JSON Schema structured output through OpenRouter, so you can use GPT, Claude, Gemini, DeepSeek, Grok, or any other model that supports strict schemas. Local OpenAI-compatible servers (Ollama, LM Studio, vLLM, llama.cpp) work too.

Retry by ID, not by batch. After every response, the engine accepts only expected IDs with unique, non-empty translations. If a batch of 40 returns 35 valid results, the next request contains only the 5 missing cues. You don't pay to re-translate the whole batch, and the good results aren't thrown away.

Rebuild from the original cue list. The final SRT is assembled from the parsed source, not from whatever the model returned. One failed line can't shift or delete the cues after it. If a line still can't be translated after retries, it stays in place as an empty subtitle and gets flagged in the report, so the failure is visible instead of hidden.

Jev: automatic QC that flags, not rewrites

A complete, well-aligned file can still contain bad translations, so the engine adds a QC pass. Local deterministic checks run first and catch empty lines and structural problems without calling any model. Then Jev reviews every source–translation pair and answers one question: does this line need human review?

It's tuned to flag things like dropped meaning, reversed negation, changed names, numbers, dates, or units, and truncated or repeated text. It looks at neighbouring cues in the batch, so a sentence that legitimately spans several cues isn't flagged. The rules favour precision: style differences pass, so the report stays short enough that you'll actually read it.

Jev doesn't rewrite anything. A flag means "look at this line", not "this line is wrong". The review rules live in qc.py if you want to see exactly what it checks or tune it.

Quick start

You'll need Python 3.10+ and an OpenRouter API key. On macOS or Linux:

git clone https://github.com/GeekLinkDev/jev-subtitle-translator.git
cd jev-subtitle-translator
bash run_web.sh

Open http://127.0.0.1:8000, upload an SRT, pick your languages, and click Translate + QC. You can also QC an existing translation without re-translating it. You get the translated SRT plus a JSON report with line-level translation and review status.

Prefer the terminal? There's a CLI for pipelines:

export OPENROUTER_API_KEY="your-api-key"

.venv/bin/jev-subtitle-translator translate input.srt \
  --source-language en --target-language de \
  --model openai/gpt-4o-mini --output translated.srt

That writes translated.srt and translated.srt.qc.json. Point --base-url and --qc-base-url at a local server to run everything locally.

Where this fits

This repo covers one job: translating and reviewing existing SRT files. If you're starting from a video, the GeekLink desktop app for Mac and Windows is built on the same engine and adds OCR extraction of hardcoded (burned-in) subtitles, local Whisper transcription, and a bilingual editor for fixing lines side by side.

Contributions welcome

The most useful contributions are real subtitle files that break things: odd SRT formatting, language pairs where Jev misfires, or models that keep dropping IDs. Open an issue or PR on GitHub. And if you've been translating subtitles with a one-off script and your fingers crossed, give the repo a try and a star.

title: Shipping Ming-Image Design: size the card by its files, and check the alpha in code
summary:
Say you want an image endpoint for app mockups, slides and stickers, and Ming-Image-0.1-Design from inclusionAI looks like the right fit. It is MIT licensed and trained for layouts full of text. Its PNGs always carry an alpha channel, a fourth layer that stores the opacity of every pixel. Before you ship it, three things decide whether it behaves: which GPU you rent, how you phrase the transparency request, and what happens when a result is too big to send back.

We ran it on one NVIDIA A100 80GB on our cloud and wrote up every number in the Ming-Image Design test on one A100.

Budget memory from the component list

The model card calls it a 6B model. That figure covers only the diffusion transformer, the part that refines random noise into an image step by step, and it is 12.3 GB on disk. The repository also ships a 34 GB language model that interprets the prompt, a 6.2 GB connector between the two and a 0.25 GB decoder that produces the pixels: 52.9 GB in total.

Once loaded, the model held 46.3 GiB of GPU memory before drawing anything. A 1024 x 1024 image peaked at 50.45 GiB, and a 2048 x 2048 one reached 64.4 GiB. That lines up with the authors' GitHub README, where the smallest setup they validated is one GPU with at least 80 GiB. If your capacity planning starts from a parameter count, add up the folder sizes first.

We also planned to fake a 24 GB card by capping the A100's memory. An open bug kept the new setting from reaching the running model, so nothing under 80 GB is tested.

Treat transparency as a prompt format you have to test

inclusionAI lists ten trigger phrases for transparent output and asks you to open the prompt with a single one. There is no special code path: the decoder always emits four channels, and transparency happens only if the model draws it.

We wrote the request six different ways, and a single version produced a cutout. It started with "RGBA, 4-channel, transparent background" as a line by itself, followed by the fox sticker description: 83.2 % of pixels came out fully transparent. Put a comma after the phrase instead and the fox sat on opaque white, with a minimum alpha of 247. Yet the same newline trick on an app icon still gave a solid background. The newline helped the fox, and it guarantees nothing.

The practical rule is to stop trusting the request and measure the response:

prompt = "RGBA, 4-channel, transparent background\n" + description  # newline, not ", "
alpha = np.asarray(Image.open("out.png").getchannel("A"))
transparent = (alpha == 0).mean()  # fox with newline: 0.832, with a comma: 0.0

Retry or reject below a threshold that fits your assets. Our backend (the small server that keeps the model in memory and serves requests) returns this fraction with every image.

Quoted strings are the spec, the rest is filler

In 5 of our 7 layouts, every string we put in quotes was correct. Anything unspecified, such as chart axes or feature cards, filled up with pseudo-words that pass at a glance.

Long lists slip. A 12-line menu asked for in two columns came out in one, with two wrong prices and an invented line. If your output carries prices, someone has to read every line. inclusionAI suggests first rewriting prompts into a structured, Figma-style description with another language model; we did not try that.

Three settings that bite between the model and your client

What Why it matters
12 steps, guidance 1.0 Steps are drawing passes; guidance is how hard the prompt steers them. The authors validated these. Our panel's image tester defaults to 20 and 4.5.
1024 and 2048 only It draws at the closer level, then resizes: a 1920 x 1080 slide is drawn at 1024.
Result size Our test setup accepted answers up to 8 MB. Two busy 2048 images went over, got discarded, and the client sat until a 300-second timeout.

Resolution alone does not predict file size: other 2048 images fit. The SDK example's backend now lowers WebP quality until the file fits, tested on saved images only. The long platform wait is still open, and we did not check the hosted limit.

Speed with the authors' untuned script: 6.2 to 7.4 seconds of GPU time per 1024 image over 10 runs, 35.8 seconds per 2048 image. The vLLM-Omni serving engine reports about 2.2 seconds at 1024 on two H100s; we did not run it.

What this does not prove

These are observations, not a quality score: 15 images, one try per prompt, prompts we wrote, one seed (the random starting point), a single GPU model, and requests sent one by one. We did not call the hosted service.

On Python 3.11 the authors' pinned versions did not run as written; slightly newer numpy and torch fixed it. The dependency fixes, per-size memory figures and the full transparency table sit in the engineering appendix. To compare text rendering, our MOSS-Image hands-on test measured the same kind of layouts on one A40.

Credit where it belongs. inclusionAI made Ming-Image-0.1-Design and released it under MIT, inference code and transparency phrases included. It reuses pieces from other teams: Ling for the language model, Qwen2.5 for vision, Qwen2 for the connector, Z-Image for the transformer design and Qwen-Image for the decoder. The vLLM-Omni team contributed a serving recipe plus benchmark numbers, hugging-apps a demo Space, and the AI Search channel is where we first saw the model. We wrote the custom backend, deployed it, fixed the dependencies and took the measurements. Timings, sample images and the deploy walkthrough live in the Ming-Image Design research article on inferencekey.com.
